{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=research+agenda+revision+sunk+cost+epistemic+commitments+question+abandonment&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.23943/princeton/9780691167237.003.0005\", \"title\": [\"Hinge Commitments\"], \"abstract\": \"

This chapter explores a fourth way of casting the Wittgensteinian account of the structure of rational evaluation. Like the nonpropositional reading used to tackle the account's “closure problem” in the previous chapter, this fourth method is a nonepistemic proposal in that it does not treat our hinge commitments as being in the market for rationally grounded knowledge. Unlike the nonpropositional reading, however, it is not allied to additional philosophical theses that are independently controversial. With this construal of our hinge commitments in place, the chapter further explores the anti-skeptical ramifications of this proposal, including in contrast to superficially similar anti-skeptical stances.

payload.content: {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=preference+formation+memory+dependent+decisions+path+dependence+longitudinal+behavior+active+learning&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Closing the Loop on the Cocktail Party Effect: From Attention Decoding to Neuro-Steered Selective Hearing.\", \"abstract\": \"Selective hearing in multi-talker environments remains a central challenge for assistive listening technologies: conventional devices improve audibility but cannot infer which talker the listener intends to follow. This Perspective examines the emerging transition from auditory attention decoding to neuro-steered selective hearing. We argue that a recent real-time intracranial proof-of-principle study marks an important inflection point in this transition, because it shows, under high-fidelity recordings from neurosurgical patients and in controlled two-talker conditions, that decoded neural attention can be coupled online to relative-gain control, thereby improving speech perception and reducing listening effort within that experimental setting. Building on this proof of principle, we argue that the field should move beyond offline decoding accuracy as its primary benchmark and instead treat neuro-steered hearing as a closed-loop translational problem linking neural inference, acoustic scene analysis, and control policy. From this perspective, future benchmarks should integrate device-level control metrics, including latency, effective switch time, false-switch rate and recovery after erroneous updates, with listener-centered outcomes such as speech intelligibility, listening effort, user preference and everyday benefit. Accordingly, we outline a staged roadmap for electroencephalography-based systems, from controlled two-speaker paradigms to scene-aware control and ultimately wearable real-world implementations. We also discuss the complementary roles of magnetoencephalography, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, and functional magnetic resonance imaging in defining the neural mechanisms and design constraints of future systems. Overall, this Perspective frames neuro-steered selective hearing as a systems-level research pathway for evaluating whether neural attention signals can be translated into practical assistive listening technologies.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/biology15141148\", \"pmid\": \"42510695\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13406005\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/biology15141148\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13406005\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": Agriculture and Smart Breeding: A Review of SDN/NFV-Enabled Intelligent Resource Management\", \"abstract\": null, \"doi\": null, \"pmid\": \"PMC13667718\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13667718\", \"source\": \"PMC\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"PubMedCentral\", \"url\": \"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13667718/?tool=EBI\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"PubMedCentral\", \"url\": \"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13667718/pdf/?tool=EBI\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13667718\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13667718?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Epigenetic Viral Mimicry in Neuroinflammation: Retrotransposons, cGAS-STING and Microglial Hysteresis.\", \"abstract\": \"Endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), LINE-1 elements, and other endogenously active transposable-element families are now being studied for their role as a potential interface between epigenetic control and innate immunity. Here, we discuss how locus-specific failures in repressive complexes containing ATRX-DAXX-H3.3 and TRIM28-SETDB1-H3K9me3 may allow these elements to enter into unique molecular states that include double-stranded RNA, DNA/RNA hybrid molecules, RNA-protein complexes, reverse-transcription products, and RNA. Each of these states differs from the others in terms of its persistence, structural characteristics, and accessibility to sensors such as MDA5, RIG-I, cGAS-STING, and ZBP1, as well as host restriction pathways. We also emphasize that simply expressing a retroelement does not imply that it is competent to bind to a sensor and/or undergo productive retrotransposition. Rather, a distinction needs to be made between intermediate stages in the process of retrotransposition and productive retrotransposition itself. Therefore, the evidence needed to assign a specific sensor to a particular retroelement product must be presented. Furthermore, persistent stress caused by retroelement activity could converge with multiple cellular processes, such as p53-CDKN1A/p21-mediated cell-cycle arrest, PML-mediated nuclear organization, and lysosomal or metabolism-based changes leading to long-lived microglial states; however, demonstrating path dependence after removing the initiating perturbation would be required to demonstrate true hysteresis. Finally, downstream activation of complement pathways could have effects on synaptic function via separate CR3-dependent, trafficking-based, and contact-regulatory mechanisms. Overall, we recommend a locus-specific, structure-specific, and time-course-resolved approach for determining how the various states of endogenously active retroelements cross the genome-immunity boundary and contribute to neuroinflammatory dysfunction.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/medsci14060635\", \"pmid\": \"42930554\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13706720\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/medsci14060635\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13706720\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13706720?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Non-Destructive Sensing and Intelligent Quality Prediction During Fruit Drying: From Quality Formation to Decision Support.\", \"abstract\": \"Fruit drying transforms a living, water-rich tissue into a stable food through coupled changes in moisture distribution, structure, color, nutrients, and aroma. Although drying technologies and non-destructive sensing have advanced rapidly, these fields have largely developed in parallel, leaving the relationship between quality formation and measurable process signals insufficiently resolved. Here, physical and chemical changes during drying are connected to the signals that can support quality prediction. Current evidence shows that moisture loss and surface appearance are the most tractable real-time targets. Texture, bioactive retention, and flavor remain less accessible because their signals depend more strongly on internal structure, reference chemistry, or sensory response. Optical, magnetic-resonance, thermal, volatile-sensing, and electrical approaches consequently provide complementary rather than interchangeable views of the product. Multimodal models improve prediction when the added signals resolve different aspects of drying, but redundant inputs can increase complexity without improving transferability. Progress toward intelligent fruit drying therefore depends on matching sensors to the evolving product state, validating models beyond individual batches and instruments, and linking predictions to practical process decisions. This process-quality perspective provides a basis for moving from retrospective quality assessment toward reliable monitoring and controlled drying.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/foods15173122\", \"pmid\": \"42737365\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13565016\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/foods15173122\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13565016\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13565016?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "de8522e5fb7513f032ca9d6bf84239853e778535cf9bc3c270e951df70e86ac9", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.3390/biology15141148", "doi:10.3390/medsci14060635", "doi:10.3390/foods15173122", "pmc:PMC13406005", "pmc:PMC13667718", "pmc:PMC13706720", "pmc:PMC13565016"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.3390/biology15141148", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13406005", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13406005?pdf=render", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13667718/?tool=EBI", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13667718/pdf/?tool=EBI", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13667718", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13667718?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3390/medsci14060635"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
